newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - German cycles.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - German cycles.

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN
Those in the German insurance industry dreaming of an imminent upward swing in the insurance cycle will most probably be in for a rude awakening.

Judging by the first market figures released by the German insurance association Gesamtverband der Deutschen Versicherungswirtschaft (GDV), the market is likely to take a further dive. Motor prices are falling again this year, as are rates for industrial insurance. In all property and casualty lines together, GDV expects zero growth.

But most alarming for those who believe in a fast-moving cycle must be the fact that German insurers, as a whole, did quite well in both motor and industrial lines - despite the serious price war that they have been fighting for nearly two years now.
In motor, rebate schemes, price cuts, new tariffs and much poaching of customers did not prevent the market as a whole from producing an underwriting profit.

Admittedly, it is much smaller than in earlier years, and partly due to luck - for example the absence of major hail or storm events. But the fact that the underwriting result is still in profit means that there is a lot of room for further price cuts - which companies are busily dishing out, in order to keep their market share.

Industrial lines, too, seem to have performed better than expected. All industrial property together last year produced an underwriting profit of gross 150 million marks, after 220 million marks in 1995. Again, there is still room for manoeuvre, and Allianz' announcement that from April onwards it will (for free) insure certain risk components so far covered separately is another shot in the battle.

It is important to remember, though, that the results differ widely between companies. While the market is still producing underwriting profits in motor, some players are seriously considering withdrawing from this segment due to their heavy losses.

Moreover, much of the current positive result stems from settlement profits, from the fat that was gathered in earlier, better years and is now melting away. The present allocations to claims reserves are much smaller. Some companies, and their shareholders, therfore may be in for a nasty surprise in one or two years' time.
